cases.title: Enron Dabhol power plant: police beat and arrest protesting villagers
cases.place: Dabhol power project, Guhagar, Ratnagiri District, Maharashtra, India
cases.point: Dabhol plant area on the Konkan coast, Ratnagiri District (approximate)

lenders.name: Export-Import Bank of the United States
lenders.role: Extended a loan guarantee of about US$290 million in late 1994 for Phase I. HRW says its involvement and OPIC's were suspended in May 1998, so both came before the 1997 police actions. The State Department told it there was no objection on human rights grounds (Human Rights Watch).

lenders.name: Overseas Private Investment Corporation (US; now DFC)
lenders.role: Gave about US$100 million in political risk insurance for Phase I. Enron reportedly filed a claim of about US$200 million with it on 17 January 2002 (Human Rights Watch).

lenders.name: Private foreign investors led by Bank of America and ABN Amro
lenders.role: Provided about US$150 million for Phase I (Human Rights Watch).

cases.conditions: Power plant built by Dabhol Power Corporation, owned 80% by Enron and 10% each by General Electric and Bechtel at the time of the 1999 report. Phase I cost US$920 million. The World Bank had refused to finance it as "not economically viable" (Human Rights Watch).
cases.community: From 1992 local people opposed the project over land taken from farmers, diverted water, environmental risks and alleged corruption (Human Rights Watch).
cases.suppression: In May 1997 police beat and arrested nearly 180 peaceful protesters outside the company gates. In June 1997 Maharashtra police raided a fishing village and beat and arrested dozens; Sadhana Bhalekar, three months pregnant, was dragged into the street and beaten with batons. Contractors to the company harassed and attacked opponents. From 1994 the company used Section 47 of the Bombay Police Act to pay 125 rupees a day per officer for police stationed at the site, between 10 and 300 at a time (Human Rights Watch).
cases.outcome: Protests had largely ended by 1998. Maharashtra ended its agreement in June 2001 over the high cost of the power, and Enron declared bankruptcy on 2 December 2001 (Human Rights Watch).

sources.title: Enron: History of Human Rights Abuse in India

cases.confidence_note: Rests on Human Rights Watch field research. The company told Amnesty International in November 1997 that it did not employ, second or subcontract police at the site, and that it "would not tolerate any human rights abuses" by staff and sub-contractors. HRW found no evidence the company approved specific criminal acts by contractors.
cases.ecosystem: Konkan coast, fishing villages and farmland

cases.title: TIPNIS road, signed Brazilian loan: police break up the Chaparina march
cases.place: La Chaparina, near Yucumo, Beni, Bolivia
cases.point: Camp of the Eighth Indigenous March at La Chaparina, near Yucumo (approximate)

lenders.name: Brazilian Development Bank (BNDES)
lenders.role: Signed a loan contract for up to US$332 million on 15 February 2011, approved by Bolivia's Law 112 of 7 May 2011, so it was in force at the 25 September 2011 police action. BNDES never released any money for the highway (Mongabay). It cancelled in 2012 (Los Tiempos; Conectas); Mongabay dates the formal end to September 2013.

cases.conditions: Loan contract covering 80% of the US$415 million, 306 km Villa Tunari-San Ignacio de Moxos highway. The Brazilian firm OAS held the building contract. Segment II, about 177 km, would have cut through TIPNIS, a national park and indigenous territory (Agência Brasil; Plataforma BNDES statement carried by IHU).
cases.community: About 800 marchers, mostly indigenous and including women and children, were attacked on 25 September 2011. Mothers and children were separated and put on eight buses towards Yucumo; a preliminary list from the group Fobomade named dozens missing, including children (Plataforma BNDES statement carried by IHU). Official counts of injured or detained were not found.
cases.suppression: About 500 police raided the camp on 25 September 2011 with tear gas and arrested leaders, who were then freed by townspeople of Rurrenabaque (Eurasia Review). The Plataforma BNDES statement adds batons and says the camp was set on fire (IHU). A peer-reviewed study describes armed forces dispersing the march (Contexto Internacional).
cases.killed_note: No deaths are reported in these sources.
cases.outcome: Four officials resigned, including the defense and government ministers. President Morales denied ordering the operation and apologized. He signed a law suspending the road, reported 27 October 2011 (Eurasia Review; Agência Brasil). Campaigners wrote to BNDES on 25 August 2011 asking it to suspend financing; the Plataforma BNDES reported no reply.

A study citing a Constitutional Court resolution dates a contract with OAS and BNDES to 2009; a financing protocol was signed on 22 August 2009 (Mongabay).

cases.title: Punta Catalina coal plant: European bank loan with Italian state cover, ash mounds
cases.place: Catalina, Peravia province (Baní), Dominican Republic
cases.point: Punta Catalina plant area, Catalina district, Peravia (approximate)

lenders.name: Société Générale, Deutsche Bank, ING, Santander, UniCredit
lenders.role: Bank group lending US$632.5 million. It paid US$200 million on 30 December 2015 and had reached US$361 million by 30 September 2016, including the insurance premium (Diario Libre; elDinero).

lenders.name: SACE (Italian export credit agency)
lenders.role: Guaranteed the European bank loan (Diario Libre; elDinero).

lenders.name: Brazilian Development Bank (BNDES)
lenders.role: Separate US$656 million loan, approved by Congress in 2015. Not a cent had been paid by June 2016 (Diario Libre), and the state moved to replace it with US$600 million in bonds after it failed (elDinero, October 2016). Not shown to have paid.

cases.conditions: Two coal units at Punta Catalina, with state utility CDEEE handling the loans and Odebrecht leading construction. Two external credits totalled US$1,288.51 million (Diario Libre). The plant was finished in 2020 (FIDH).

companies.name: Odebrecht
companies.role: Lead builder; FIDH says it paid bribes of over US$39.5 million tied to the tender and construction

cases.community: FIDH, CNLCC and INSAPROMA report three ash mounds in Catalina totalling over 600,000 tonnes near water sources and farmland, with storms carrying ash onto water and land (FIDH, 2023). In December 2020 the energy minister announced an emergency plan for the ash yard, and the plant's administrator spoke of inherited disorder in ash handling (elDinero). A complaint by INSAPROMA, backed by hundreds of residents, cites farming and fishing losses and seeks removal of ash at San José batey and US$3 billion (Dominican Today, 2025). Farmers in Nizao claim over US$6.3 million for crop losses within five kilometres (Acento, 2025).
cases.killed_note: FIDH projects about 6,000 premature deaths over 30 years. This is a projection, not a count of deaths, and is not counted.
cases.outcome: The 2023 report went to the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child. The 2025 complaint went to the anti-corruption prosecutor's office, and no ruling was reported. An injunction sought in December 2015 is mentioned in the campaigners' letter; its result was not found.

Société Générale said in 2016 the project complied with its coal policy and that no bribery rules were broken.

cases.title: Sondu-Miriu dam: Japanese loans, land and a dispute over the river
cases.place: Sondu-Miriu hydropower project, Nyakach, western Kenya
cases.point: Sondu-Miriu project area, Nyakach (approximate)

lenders.name: Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC; now JICA)
lenders.role: ODA loans: Phase I ¥6,933 million and Phase II ¥10,554 million (JICA). About 80% of funding came from Japan (FoE Japan). Japan suspended funding in 2001 over environmental disruption and corruption (Corpwatch).

cases.conditions: Japanese loans to KenGen, the state power company, for a 60 MW plant. Funds first moved in 1997 and work began in March 1999 (Corpwatch).

companies.name: KenGen
companies.role: Kenyan state power company, borrower and builder

cases.community: FoE Japan reported about 1,000 households displaced by January 2001 and unfair compensation. Campaigners said hillside streams dried after tunnel blasting at Kasaye, and reported chest illnesses (Corpwatch). JICA counts land compensation for 649 households (213.2 ha, about 91 million KSh) and 1,714 more along the power line (137 million KSh), says relocations were not recorded and most stayed nearby. A March 2012 reading downstream was 1.4 m³/s against a recommended 3.0; JICA calls it a possibly single dry-season reading and says monthly averages stayed above 3.0.
cases.suppression: Protests met violence from police and KenGen guards, and four Japanese and four Kenyan journalists were arrested (FoE Japan). At least one man was severely wounded after days in custody (Corpwatch).
cases.killed_note: The group Africa Water Network claimed two deaths since building began (Corpwatch). Not verified and not counted.
cases.outcome: Phase II loan was signed only in July 2009, more than five years late (JICA). A technical committee was set up but could not enforce decisions; 81.9% of surveyed households who knew of it were dissatisfied (JICA).

sources.title: Sondu-Miriu Hydropower Project: background

Kenya: Japan Suspends Funding for Sondu Miriu Dam

cases.confidence_note: JICA's evaluators found no serious harm to the natural environment, could not tie dust-related illness or dirty water to the project, and blamed lower fish catches on other causes; 70% of 200 surveyed households were satisfied. FoE Japan and Kenyan groups describe displacement, lost water and repression.
cases.ecosystem: Sondu River and Kasaye Hills

lvwhy.land: Land was taken for the works and the power line.

cases.title: Upper Atbara and Setit dams: Gulf and Arab funds, tens of thousands moved
cases.place: Upper Atbara and Setit dam complex, Kassala and El Gedaref states, Sudan
cases.point: Rumela and Burdana dam area on the Kassala-El Gedaref border (approximate)

lenders.name: Arab Fund for Economic and Social Development
lenders.role: Loans 557/2010, 566/2011 and a supplementary KD 30 million loan; together about 22% of the KD 512.6 million cost (Arab Fund).

lenders.name: Kuwait Fund, Saudi Fund for Development, Islamic Development Bank, OPEC Fund, Government of Algeria
lenders.role: Together about KD 175 million, roughly 34% of the cost (Arab Fund). The OPEC Fund share was US$30 million, signed 24 February 2012 (OPEC Fund).

lenders.name: Government of China
lenders.role: About KD 29.2 million, about 7% of the cost at the time of the first Arab Fund loan (Arab Fund); listed as co-financier by the OPEC Fund.

cases.conditions: Two connected dams and a 320 MW plant. The Arab Fund's project page includes land acquisition, property compensation and resettlement of about 138,000 inhabitants.
cases.community: Moves began in February 2015 with 500 families from the Wad El Helew area; a resident said the dam management began flooding lands without keeping its commitments (Radio Dabanga). The Niles records residents moved to new towns from 2012. Radio Dabanga cites representatives of 30,000 displaced families. By March 2016 a displaced representative said 25% of those due compensation had not been paid and half of farmers had not been paid for lost land. In December 2015 villagers reported four months without water or electricity. About 11,000 acres of farmland were taken for resettlement; residents reported high unemployment and poverty (Radio Dabanga). The Niles quotes residents saying promised equipment never came and that 700 families in one neighbourhood lost their rights.
cases.suppression: Sudan's security service (NISS) detained 27 residents at their farms in July 2017; a member of the El Gedaref parliament said the pretext was that the farms had been taken for the Electricity Ministry. Relatives said they were held in El Gedaref prison without visits (Radio Dabanga).
cases.outcome: First turbine inaugurated in February 2017 (The Niles). A youth leader said a justice ministry arbitration panel refused farmland compensation in some areas, calling the land private residential sectors, and left out Kuna Zuberma, about 650 families (Radio Dabanga). The OPEC Fund lists its loan as completed.

cases.title: Tendaho sugar project: India's credit line and Afar grazing land
cases.place: Tendaho sugar project, Afar region, Ethiopia
cases.point: Tendaho sugar area, Awash valley, Afar (approximate)

lenders.name: Export-Import Bank of India
lenders.role: US$640 million credit announced 14 January 2008 for Ethiopia's sugar expansion, with a new factory at Tendaho (Sudan Tribune); a loan at 1.75% (US embassy cable). The Reporter says the bank financed the Tendaho project, and an Exim official said most sugar projects it finances underperform. Its largest single line of credit at the time (Business Standard).

cases.conditions: Sugar expansion costing about US$1.3 billion, with Ethiopia covering the other US$660 million (Sudan Tribune). The Centre for Financial Accountability says Exim invests in Tendaho through the Indian firm Overseas Infrastructure Alliance.

companies.name: Overseas Infrastructure Alliance
companies.role: Indian firm on the Tendaho project

cases.community: A 2008 Addis Ababa University thesis says the irrigable and reservoir areas cover land normally used for grazing, that Dubti pastoralists lost grazing to the main canal, and that watering sources were reduced. An NGO, citing a November 2016 thesis, says most Afar grazing land was taken and sugarcane caused water shortages for homes and livestock, and that the community says it was not consulted (Centre for Financial Accountability).
cases.outcome: A US embassy cable records a government statement that 10,000 hectares were set aside for pastoralists. A 2007 warning by the Afar Human Rights Organization that up to 500,000 could be displaced was a forecast; no count of people actually displaced by the sugar project was found. A separate 2014 study of 70 respondents found 74.3% reported better livelihoods from the irrigation project.

cases.title: Upper Kotmale dam: Japanese loans, 524 households moved
cases.place: Talawakele, Nuwara Eliya District, Sri Lanka
cases.point: Talawakele reservoir area (approximate)

lenders.name: Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC; now JICA)
lenders.role: ODA loans: Phase I ¥33,265 million (March 2002) and Phase II ¥4,552 million (March 2010) (JICA).

cases.conditions: Loans to the Ceylon Electricity Board for a 150 MW plant with a headrace tunnel of 12.5 km (JICA; the Sunday Times says 12.9 km).
cases.community: 524 households were resettled, most of them Tamil tea estate workers. Some households said dynamite blasting cracked their walls. Average flow at St. Clair's Falls was 13.45 m³/s before the project; the electricity board now releases 1.31 m³/s in daytime (JICA). The Japanese NGO JACSES says residents were "seriously affected", and reports that blasting victims were not told how to claim, that a Hindu temple plot was too small, and that Nanu Oya residents must carry water up a steep slope from the river.
cases.outcome: JICA rated the project satisfactory. Two former committee members said about 100 complaints were all resolved; the electricity board assessed damage and paid for wall repairs; 66% of surveyed people thought compensation sufficient, 18% did not.

cases.title: AES coal ash from Puerto Rico dumped at Arroyo Barril and Manzanillo
cases.place: Arroyo Barril, Samaná, Dominican Republic
cases.point: Arroyo Barril on Samaná Bay, one of two dump sites; the other is Manzanillo (approximate)

lenders.name: AES Corp. (United States; foreign company)
lenders.role: The suit names AES Corp. and its subsidiaries over ash from its coal plant at Guayama, Puerto Rico, hauled by a contractor (Grist). No lender involved.

cases.conditions: Foreign company, not a loan. The complaint says AES chose Dominican beaches as the cheapest option (Grist). Contractor Roger Fina, who hauled the ash, says it was meant for asphalt (Grist). The parents also allege bribes to local officials (Courthouse News).

companies.name: AES Corp.
companies.role: Owner of the Guayama plant that produced the ash

cases.community: Between October 2003 and March 2004 ash was left on two Dominican beaches: about 160 million pounds in the lawsuit (Grist), about 54,000 tons in Dominican reporting (Dominican Today). Half of 42 nearby residents tested had unsafe blood arsenic levels, the complaint says. Parents allege miscarriages, severe birth defects and infant deaths; residents report breathing illness and rashes (Grist; Courthouse News).
cases.killed_note: A Delaware lawsuit alleged three stillbirths or child deaths in the first of seven cases (Dominican Today). It settled without a verdict in available reporting, so these are not counted.
cases.outcome: In 2004 the Dominican government found the dumping broke its law and the Basel Convention (Grist). In a 2007 agreement the state received about US$6 million from AES and agreed to take on other lawsuits (Dominican Today). A Delaware judge announced a settlement with the plaintiffs' lawyers. INSAPROMA's president says the state paid US$37 million to 41 people in August 2016 (Dominican Today).

cases.title: Manus detention centre: Reza Barati killed under G4S security
cases.place: Manus Island Regional Processing Centre, Papua New Guinea
cases.point: Lombrum area, Manus Island, site of the centre (approximate)

lenders.name: Government of Australia
lenders.role: Paid for the offshore centre; G4S's contract was worth about A$244 million (RAID).

lenders.name: G4S (United Kingdom)
lenders.role: G4S Australia, wholly owned by G4S plc, ran management and security from October 2012 to March 2014 (RAID).

cases.conditions: An outside government's money and a foreign company, not a loan. Australia held asylum seekers in Papua New Guinea under a private contract.
cases.community: Three days of rioting in February 2014 during severe overcrowding left Iranian asylum seeker Reza Barati, 23, dead and at least 69 injured (RAID; SBS); the Cornall review counted 62 injured (The Conversation). Physical security arrangements were lacking, and detainees got little information on their claims (The Conversation).
cases.suppression: A PNG police spokesman said in preliminary findings that local G4S guards carried out the suppression (Fairfax, Area News). The Cornall review found unclear roles between G4S and PNG police and recommended that the successor firm Transfield dismiss anyone implicated in assaults (The Conversation).
cases.killed_note: Barati was killed on 17 February 2014. Papua New Guinea's National Court convicted Louie Efi, employed by Loda Security and subcontracted to G4S, who dropped a large stone on him, and Joshua Kaluvia, a Salvation Army worker, who struck him with timber. Both were sentenced on 19 April 2016 to 10 years, five suspended. The court said expatriate and national G4S guards also kicked him. Counted because the man who struck the final blow was a guard working for G4S.
cases.outcome: RAID and the Human Rights Law Centre complained under the OECD Guidelines in September 2014; Australia's contact point rejected it as commentary on government policy. A class action for 1,900 detainees was filed in December 2016 against Australia, G4S and Transfield (RAID).

G4S was a contractor to Australia, and it passes here as the foreign operator of the centre whose guards took part. cases.title: Mangaung private prison: G4S accused of electroshocks and forced injections
cases.place: Mangaung Correctional Centre, Bloemfontein, South Africa
cases.point: Bloemfontein, seat of the prison (approximate)

lenders.name: G4S (United Kingdom; foreign company)
lenders.role: Has run the prison since 2001, one of two private prisons in South Africa (TimesLIVE).

cases.conditions: Foreign company running a state prison under contract; the government decided in 2010 against further prison partnerships (TimesLIVE).
cases.community: A 12-month Wits Justice Project investigation, published October 2013, alleged excessive electroshocks and forced injections of antipsychotic drugs. Leaked video showed inmate Bheki Dlamini forced onto a bed and injected by the emergency security team. Inmates said they were locked up about 23 hours a day (Mail & Guardian). The prison holds about 3,000 (TimesLIVE).
cases.suppression: 22 inmates were moved to Kokstad super-maximum prison on 11 November 2013 and held in isolation for eight months, never formally charged, they say (Mail & Guardian).
cases.outcome: The prisons department took over in October 2013, then returned the prison to G4S after 10 months (Mail & Guardian; TimesLIVE). No G4S staff had been prosecuted, suspended or fired by October 2014 (Mail & Guardian). Leigh Day wrote a claim letter for 43 former inmates on 12 February 2015 (TimesLIVE). In 2018 the civil claim was unresolved, the department's investigation report was still unreleased, and a court case to obtain it was pending (Mail & Guardian). No court finding was found.

sources.title: No escape for abused Mangaung prisoners

Mangaung defends antipsychotic injections for prisoners

cases.confidence_note: G4S denies any assaults, torture, electroshocking or forced medication and says a separate medical facility handles clinical care. Prison medical staff told the Judicial Inspectorate the injections were clinically justified, and the inspectorate said it found no assault allegations it could verify. G4S ran the prison under a state contract; it passes here as the foreign operator whose own staff are accused, and the case stays contested because no court has ruled.

lvwhy.priv: A state prison was run by a foreign company.

cases.title: MV Solomon Trader: bauxite ship spills oil beside East Rennell World Heritage site
cases.place: Kangava Bay, Rennell Island, Solomon Islands
cases.point: Kangava Bay, western Rennell (approximate)

lenders.name: Bintan Mining (foreign company)
lenders.role: Mined the bauxite under contract from the lease holder APID and chartered the ship to carry it (Islands Business; RNZ). APIBC lists it as British Virgin Islands; Islands Business calls it Indonesian-based.

cases.conditions: Foreign mining company, not a loan. The ship belonged to Hong Kong-based King Trader Ltd and was loading bauxite ore when it grounded during Cyclone Oma; critics asked why loading went on during cyclone warnings (RNZ; UNESCO; ITOPF).

companies.name: Bintan Mining Corporation
companies.role: Bauxite miner under contract and ship charterer

companies.name: Asia Pacific Investment Development Ltd
companies.role: Holds the mining lease; named by UNESCO among responsible parties

cases.community: The ship grounded on 4 February 2019 in poor weather. About 60 tonnes had leaked in early reports (RNZ), about 75 tonnes later (SCMP); a 2025 report says over 300 tonnes (APIBC). Beaches were covered with oil and a local leader said fishing grounds were ruined (RNZ). About 5 km of shore was affected, with clean-up until 26 July 2019 (ITOPF). About 1,200 people live in the World Heritage property next to the site (UNESCO).
cases.outcome: On 31 January 2025 four customary landowners and the Attorney-General sued King Trader, its Korean insurers and Bintan in the High Court in Honiara, seeking an estimated US$30-100 million; no compensation had been paid (APIBC).

cases.title: Vale nickel plant at Goro: acid spills kill fish in New Caledonia
cases.place: Goro plant, Prony, southern New Caledonia
cases.point: Goro plant area, North Bay (Baie Nord) creek (approximate)

lenders.name: Vale (Brazil; foreign company)
lenders.role: Owned the US$6 billion plant, in production from 2010, until the 2021 transfer to Prony Resources (Mongabay; ECA Watch).

cases.conditions: Foreign company, not a loan. ECA Watch says indigenous groups earlier lobbied France to withdraw a US$500 million tax subsidy, and that a court annulled the operating permit in 2006.
cases.community: Five acid leaks were recorded in the decade after 2010 (Mongabay). In May 2014 about 100,000 litres of acid-tainted effluent reached a river and killed about 1,000 fish, and the plant closed (Reuters via ECA Watch; SCMP).

cases.title: Nexen Block 14, Hadramawt: oily water floods farms
cases.place: Blocks 14 (Masila) and 51, near Raseb, Hadramawt, Yemen
cases.point: Masila area of Hadramawt (approximate)

lenders.name: Nexen (Canada; foreign company)
lenders.role: Formerly Canadian Occidental Petroleum; operated Blocks 14 and 51 in Hadramawt, later sold to China's CNOOC (OCCRP).

cases.conditions: Foreign company, not a loan.
cases.community: In March 2008 about 4,500 barrels of oily water leaked from a drainage well at Block 14 and flowed over farms for four days, tribal leader Omar Saeed Ba'abaad says; he says his farms fell from 40-50 bags of wheat a season to about 10. In Raseb, floods carried waste from open drilling pits into the valley; a report made for Yemen's parliament in 2014, with images of Nexen rig sites on Block 51, accused Nexen of "wilful negligence" with drilling fluids (OCCRP). Nexen was processing about 2 million barrels of produced water a day on Block 14 in 2008 (Sana'a Center).
cases.killed_note: Hadramawt Cancer Foundation data show cases nearly tripled between the early 2000s and 2015, but no study proves oil caused this (OCCRP). Not counted.
cases.outcome: Yemen's Oil Ministry took Nexen to arbitration in Paris. It was ordered to pay nearly US$10 million for an incinerator, equipment and an impact study, and the pollution claim was dismissed as out of time. Nexen stopped operating near Raseb in 2015. cases.title: Del Monte pineapple farm, Kenya: guards accused of killings
cases.place: Del Monte pineapple farm, Murang'a-Kiambu border, near Thika, Kenya
cases.point: Farm about 40 km northeast of Nairobi (approximate)

lenders.name: Fresh Del Monte (headquartered in the Cayman Islands; foreign company)
lenders.role: Del Monte Kenya is its subsidiary (OCCRP). Its 80 sq km farm supplies British supermarkets and employed 237 guards (TBIJ).

cases.conditions: Foreign company, not a loan.
cases.community: A Leigh Day letter lists 146 alleged incidents involving 134 people over a decade, with five rape allegations and five deaths since 2019 (TBIJ). A local group, the Kagama Community Action Forum, says it has documented over 1,860 abuses (OCCRP). In May 2024 Felister Wairimu was shot in the neck by a stray bullet on her balcony during a police clash with pineapple thieves, and at least four others were hit that week; the shooter was not identified (TBIJ).
cases.suppression: Witnesses allege Del Monte representatives offered money and jobs for supporting statements after the December 2023 deaths (TBIJ).
cases.killed_note: TBIJ reports six people allegedly killed by guards in a decade and at least five more bodies found in November-December 2023. Five former guards went on trial over Bernard Murigi Wanginye (2019). None had brought a conviction, so none is counted.
cases.outcome: In March 2024 Del Monte fired over 200 guards and brought in G4S (TBIJ). A civil claim was filed in December 2023 at Thika High Court, naming 10 people, with dozens more asking to join (OCCRP); TBIJ puts petitioners at over 2,000. Tesco, Waitrose and Asda stopped stocking the fruit. Kenya's human rights commission and the police were investigating (TBIJ), and a Senate committee was sent to investigate in October 2025 (The Star).

cases.place: Nain and Myersville, St Elizabeth, Jamaica
cases.point: JISCO Alpart refinery area, Nain (approximate)

lenders.name: Jiuquan Iron and Steel (JISCO; China, state-owned)
lenders.role: Agreed on 19 July 2016 to buy the refinery from UC Rusal for US$299 million (Aluminium Today; Office of the Prime Minister of Jamaica), and put in a further US$60 million (Dialogue Earth).

cases.community: Residents of seven communities report nausea, worse asthma and lung infections, and dust in the rain tanks they rely on (Dialogue Earth). Jamaica's environment agency NEPA served JISCO 16 enforcement orders, alleging poor management of its 350-hectare waste area and permit breaches (Dialogue Earth). cases.outcome: In February 2020 some payment was agreed for people hit in December and January. Local leaders say moving those in the dust path is the only long-term answer; no date was set (Jamaica Observer). Claimants must sign a release; one was offered US$60 against US$152 spent on glasses (Dialogue Earth).

cases.title: Pueblo Viejo gold mine: families below the El Llagal tailings dam
cases.place: La Piñita, La Cerca and Los Naranjos, near Cotuí, Dominican Republic
cases.point: Pueblo Viejo mine area near Cotuí (approximate)

lenders.name: Barrick Gold (Canada; foreign company)
lenders.role: Runs the mine through a joint venture with Newmont; took it over around 2006 and invested about US$4 billion (Jacobin).

cases.conditions: Foreign companies, not a loan.
cases.community: About 450 families from six villages, within a group of about 2,000 people, report losing livestock, cacao and fruit, with cacao down at least 40% by an activist's estimate, and report lesions, breathing and stomach problems. Tests in 2014 on residents of four villages found high cyanide and heavy metals, though the article does not name who ran them, and a 2012 Dominican Academy of Sciences report said the mine was contaminating the Hatillo dam (Jacobin). cases.suppression: National police fired tear gas at protesters at a Barrick meeting in Yamasá in April 2021 (Jacobin).

In June 2025 the government, residents and Barrick signed a resettlement agreement tied to the mine's expansion and new dam, without mention of contamination (elDinero). The community spokesperson says about 450 families below El Llagal still lack adequate protection.

cases.community: On 16 May 2013 a concrete ceiling used to store materials fell on workers; ten were injured, the minister said (RFA). Early reports gave two dead: Al Jazeera gave at least two dead and six injured.
cases.killed_note: Three workers, two at the scene and one in hospital, confirmed by Social Affairs Minister Ith Samheng (RFA; Irish Times). Al Jazeera's two was an earlier count. Counted because the building was the company's, the minister blamed its construction, and the company admitted neglect (IndustryWeek).
cases.outcome: The factory had no compensation plan at first; officials promised state support for families and medical bills (RFA). The operator later said it would take full responsibility for the families of dead and injured (IndustryWeek).

lenders.name: Nien Hsing Textile (Taiwan; foreign owner)
lenders.role: Taiwan-based owner of C&Y Garments, Global Garments and Nien Hsing International, about 9,500 workers in all (Worker Rights Consortium). Levi's, Kontoor (Wrangler, Lee) and The Children's Place were buyers and are not the link.

cases.conditions: Foreign owner, not a loan.
cases.community: The Worker Rights Consortium found women in all three factories pressured into sex with managers and supervisors to get or keep jobs. It interviewed 140 workers; of 38 women interviewed in depth, 24 reported harassment or abuse they had experienced or seen. It also reports harassment by male co-workers.
cases.suppression: A worker who reported harassment was dismissed in April 2018 after a complaint from the same supervisor, and managers threatened that unionising would bring closures or job losses (Worker Rights Consortium).
cases.outcome: Nien Hsing signed a binding agreement with five unions and two women's groups, setting up an independent complaints committee; brands agreed to cut orders on material breach. Chair Richard Chen said the company was "fully committed" (City Press).

sources.title: Assessment re Nien Hsing Textile (Lesotho)

cases.confidence_note: Nien Hsing formally denied the harassment findings and said it could not verify them, then signed agreements in August 2019. Testimony is anonymous.
